summary.title: Why Can't Programmers... Program?
summary.one_liner: Learn why a simple "FizzBuzz" coding question is used to screen out job applicants who cannot write basic code, and how it fits into hiring.
takeaways: A FizzBuzz-style question (print 1 to 100 with Fizz/Buzz substitutions) is a very simple screen that many applicants reportedly fail.
Several hiring managers (Imran, Dan Kegel, and the author's company Vertigo) report that many candidates, including graduates with degrees, cannot write basic loops or use recursion.
Vertigo requires a code sample before the phone interview and includes a small coding exercise on-site, avoiding tedious puzzle questions.
The author argues that the gap between people who can program and those who cannot is large, and questions whether the profession needs more formal standards.
summary.summary: This is a short opinion blog post by Jeff Atwood on Coding Horror. He discusses reports from hiring managers, including Imran, Dan Kegel, and a commenter, that many programming job applicants cannot solve trivial tasks like printing FizzBuzz, writing a loop from 1 to 10, or using recursion. The post describes the FizzBuzz question as a deliberately easy screening tool and explains how Vertigo uses code samples and a small on-site coding exercise instead. It closes by wondering whether formal software engineering professionalization, as Steve McConnell advocated, could help.
